p: Nannaya began the translation from Sanskrit at the request of the king, and his part marks the earliest known beginning of a written literary tradition in Telugu. It is composed in the Champu style and is so polished that several scholars think it probable that literary works existed in Telugu before him. No such writings have been found, apart from references to songs and poems and some verses in inscriptions, and Telugu tradition honours him as the Adi Kavi, the first poet.

Tikkana, who lived from 1205 to 1288, was born into a Niyogi Brahmin family and was a minister of the Nellore Chola ruler Manumasiddhi II. Errana, also called Yerrapragada, was a poet at the court of King Prolaya Vema Reddy, who reigned from 1325 to 1353 and founded the Reddy dynasty; he bore the titles Prabandha-parameshvara and Shambhudasudu, servant of Shiva.

The work is not a stanza-by-stanza translation but a Telugu rendering that keeps the core narrative of the Mahabharata. Nannaya wrote the Adi Parvam, the Sabha Parvam and part of the Aranya Parvam, the Book of the Forest. Tikkana wrote the fifteen books from the Virata Parvam to the Svargarohana Parvam but did not touch the half-finished third book, because it was considered inauspicious to take up what Nannaya had left incomplete. It remained unfinished for more than a century until Errana completed it. He began his portion in the style of Nannaya and ended it in the style of Tikkana, as a bridge between the two.

The Sanskrit epic is reckoned at 100 parvas and 100,000 verses. In Telugu Nannaya arranged it in eighteen parvas, divided into chapters called ashvasas, without the subdivision into upaparvas, and left out the Harivamsa; Tikkana followed his arrangement, and Errana wrote the Harivamsa as a separate work.

The three poets are revered by later Telugu poets as the Kavitrayam, the trinity of poets, and became models for all who followed. Though written by three hands over about two and a half centuries, the work is read as a single book, as if one poet had composed it in one period. Errana went on to translate the Ramayana from Sanskrit and to write an independent work, the Nrusimhapuranamu.

notes: Nannaya's dates conflict in the article: 'between 1054 and 1061 CE, when he died' in one section, '1022–1063 CE' in another. I gave no dates for him (the existing description has '11th century').
The article spells the third poet Yerrapragada / Errana / Erranna / Yerrana; I used Errana as in the existing entry. 'Sabaparvam' in the article written as 'Sabha Parvam'; 'Asvasas' as 'ashvasas'.
The article glosses Prabandha-paramēśvara as 'Master of historical anecdotes', which seems a doubtful gloss; I gave the title without it.
The paragraph on Hiranyakashipu at the end of the article belongs to Errana's other work and is left out.
